body.heading: Attention works in waves
paragraphs: Focus is not a tap that runs at one steady pressure all day. It rises, peaks and fades, and most people find somewhere between twenty and fifty minutes is a natural stretch before quality quietly drops.
Working in sprints means honouring that rhythm instead of fighting it: a defined burst of single-tasking, then a genuine break, then another burst if needed.

body.heading: Make the sprint concrete
paragraphs: Set a timer you can see, choose exactly what the sprint is for, and work only on that until the timer ends. When distracting thoughts arrive, note them on your later list and keep going — the sprint is short enough that almost everything can wait.
Start shorter than you think you should. A fifteen-minute sprint you actually do beats a heroic two-hour block you keep postponing. You can always run another sprint after the break.

body.heading: The break is part of the method
paragraphs: A break means standing up, looking at something distant, getting water, stepping outside. Scrolling a feed is not a break; it feeds your attention more of the same kind of input and leaves it just as tired.
If you return from breaks feeling no fresher, the break is too short or too screen-shaped. Adjust the break before you blame the sprint.

takeaway: Work in honest bursts, rest like you mean it, and let the rhythm carry you.
